items.title: The Influence of Workplace Spirituality and Workplace Climate on Civil Servants’ Job Performance through Intrinsic Motivation
items.abstract: This study examines the influence of workplace spirituality and workplace climate on job performance, with intrinsic motivation as a mediating variable, in public sector organizations located in Indonesia’s underdeveloped, frontier, and outermost (3T) regions. A quantitative cross-sectional approach was employed involving 342 employees of the Supiori Regency Government selected through purposive sampling. Data were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling–Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS) and Importance Performance Map Analysis (IPMA). The findings indicate that workplace spirituality and workplace climate positively and significantly affect intrinsic motivation and job performance. Workplace spirituality emerged as the strongest predictor of job performance. Intrinsic motivation also significantly mediated the relationship between workplace spirituality, workplace climate, and job performance. The IPMA results reveal that alignment with organizational values, sense of community, and employee involvement in decision-making remain priority areas for organizational improvement. This study highlights the importance of meaningful work and a supportive work environment in sustaining public sector performance within the bureaucratic context of 3T regions while extending the application of Self-Determination Theory in public sector organizations.

items.title: The Invisible Watermark: A Pilot Study on the Verifiability Gap in AI Text Watermarking
items.abstract: Article 50 of the EU AI Act requires generative AI providers to mark synthetic content in a detectable format. This obligation is carried out through a mechanism invisible to end users. The resulting gap leaves accountability around disinformation, copyright infringement, and public trust largely unaddressed. This paper reports a pilot study that probes this transparency–verifiability gap through a comparative document analysis of five major providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, xAI) combined with a small-scale empirical robustness pilot of the open-source SynthID-Text method on GPT-2. The document analysis shows that regulatory disclosure does not equate to an independently verifiable detection mechanism for third parties. In this pilot experiment, watermarked texts scored significantly higher than unwatermarked texts (t(38) = 15.94, p < 0.001, Cohen’s d = 5.04, ROC-AUC = 1.000; Youden’s J-optimal threshold = 0.533, yielding 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity on this intact (uncorrupted) sample; the design was adequately powered (80%) only for effects of d ≥ 0.91 or larger, A calibration/test-separated validation on independent held-out data (n = 320) confirmed this discrimination within the pilot setup (TPR at FPR ≤ 1% = 98.75%), without implying generalization beyond it. This signal, measured with an untrained detector, degraded substantially under a deliberately engineered high-severity stress test (50% word-level corruption), a decline confirmed by Holm-corrected pairwise comparisons across nine of the ten corruption-level pairs (F(4, 56) = 98.39, p < 0.001, generalized η2 = 0.744, r = −0.824). These are preliminary, pilot-scale findings; they indicate that Article 50 guidance should require standardized error-rate reporting and independently auditable detection access, not disclosure alone. They offer an exploratory contribution to the AI ethics literature on transparency and accountability. Given the small open-source backbones (GPT-2, with a replication on Pythia-410M), the primarily untrained detector (a small-scale trained Bayesian detector did not outperform it on intact text), the single watermarking scheme, and the largely synthetic corruption type (only one model-based paraphrase condition was tested), these results remain preliminary, pilot-scale evidence whose generalization to commercial systems, large-scale trained detectors, other watermarking families, and a broader range of realistic paraphrase and translation attacks requires future research.

items.title: The mediating role of artificial intelligence perception and creative idea generation in the impact of sustainable leadership on digital transformation and circular economy awareness
items.abstract: Introduction Today, sustainable leadership is a strategic leadership approach that addresses environmental, social, and economic priorities from a holistic perspective while at the same time driving digital transformation processes. The research aims to explain how sustainable leaders mobilize organizational resources, technological infrastructure, and human creativity within the framework of Dynamic Capabilities Theory. Methods The research was conducted on 456 white-collar employees working in small and medium-sized enterprises operating in Giresun, Kars, and Kırşehir provinces. The data collected by the convenience sampling method were analyzed using the PLS-SEM method with the SmartPLS 4.1.1 program. Results The analysis results show that sustainable leadership has significant and positive effects on perceptions of artificial intelligence, the generation of creative ideas, digital transformation, and awareness of the circular economy. It was found that the perception of artificial intelligence (AI) has a significant effect on both digital transformation and awareness of the circular economy. It was also determined that creative idea generation has significant effects on digital transformation and awareness of the circular economy. The results of the mediation analyses revealed a partial mediating role for all variables. Discussion The findings reveal that sustainable leadership is not limited to the environmental and social responsibility dimension and is a strategic element that directs digital transformation processes, shapes perceptions towards artificial intelligence, and encourages organizational creativity.

items.title: The next frontier of athletic intelligence in sports medicine and exercise science
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming sports medicine and exercise science, offering unprecedented capabilities in markerless motion capture, automated exercise prescription, diagnostic imaging and integrated athlete monitoring. These advances have the potential to democratise biomechanical analysis, scale clinical expertise to underserved populations and shift injury management from reactive treatment to predictive prevention. However, the pace of adoption carries significant risks, including technological dependency without methodological literacy, the entrenchment of global inequities through biased training datasets and models, the erosion of clinician-athlete relationships and a widening governance vacuum over data ownership and algorithmic accountability. This commentary argues that the next frontier of athletic intelligence will be defined not by technological sophistication alone, but by the wisdom, inclusivity and ethical resolve with which the sports medicine community deploys it. Disciplined engagement (rather than uncritical adoption or reflexive avoidance) is the potential path forward.

items.title: The Price of Perfection: Moral Enhancement, Free Will, and the Limits of Technological Salvation
items.abstract: In 2017, Elon Musk stated that humans must augment their mental capabilities through the “merger of biological intelligence and machine intelligence” lest they risk becoming “house cats” to artificial intelligence. In 2024, he successfully implanted his “Neuralink” chip in a human patient. Now, while the idea of improving the human condition by integrating technology into the human body did not begin with Elon Musk, his tangible advancements in neural implants have shifted the ethical questions surrounding them from theoretical to practical. One particularly thorny application of this technology—one that raises both ethical and existential questions—is its use for moral enhancement. Ethically, we must consider whether it is good or bad to employ technology that ensures individuals act morally. Existentially, if human free will is expressed most meaningfully through moral choice, should we be willing to relinquish that freedom for the sake of social harmony, crime prevention, even world peace? Or must we accept a world marked by moral failure, violence, and injustice in order to preserve human autonomy? To address these questions, I examine contemporary philosophical debates surrounding moral enhancement and place them in dialogue with classical Jewish sources. For, as will be shown, Jewish thought offers a unique framework for addressing both the ethical permissibility of moral enhancement and the existential tension between free will and moral perfection. By juxtaposing cutting-edge neurotechnology with ancient moral anthropology, this paper invites a reassessment of what it means to be human in an age increasingly capable of reshaping human agency itself.

items.abstract: This article examines the transformative impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on English language learning (ELL). It explores how AI-driven technologies—such as natural language processing (NLP), intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning algorithms, and speech recognition—facilitate personalized instruction, enhance autonomous learning, and provide immediate diagnostic feedback. Furthermore, the paper discusses the pedagogical advantages, potential limitations, and future implications of integrating AI into modern language classrooms.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Ensuring Transparency and Accountability in Corporate Social Responsibility Initiatives
items.abstract: Abstract Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) has shifted from voluntary philanthropy to a core governance domain in which stakeholders demand verifiable evidence of social and environmental performance. Yet CSR reporting remains plagued by greenwashing, inconsistent metrics, and assurance practices that are largely point-in-time and self-interested. This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can strengthen transparency and accountability in CSR initiatives. Drawing on a structured review of peer-reviewed literature and authoritative institutional reports published between 2011 and 2024, the paper develops a conceptual framework that maps four AI capabilities—natural language processing, machine-learning anomaly detection, blockchain-enabled distributed ledgers, and conversational AI—to four CSR mechanisms: dis-closure verification, real-time monitoring, traceability-based assurance, and participatory stake-holder engagement. The analysis argues that these mechanisms collectively reduce information asymmetry, harmonise divergent ESG ratings, and operationalise the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and the Artificial Intelligence Act. The paper also identifies critical limitations, including the “black-box accountability paradox”, algorithmic bias, data-quality constraints, and a widening digital divide between multinational enterprises and small and medium-sized firms. It concludes that AI is a necessary but insufficient enabler: realising its transformative potential requires combined progress on data standards, third-party model audits, regulatory sandboxes, and meaningful stakeholder participation in AI governance. Keywords: corporate social responsibility; artificial intelligence; transparency; accountability; ESG; greenwashing; blockchain; corporate governance.

items.title: The role of artificial intelligence in suicide prevention
items.abstract: Suicide is a leading cause of death, accounting for one million deaths annually worldwide (World Health Organisation, 2014). A large number of people attempt suicide, with some researchers estimating that there are approximately 25 attempts for every death (Goldsmith et al., 2002). According to the World Health Organisation, someone dies by suicide somewhere in the world every 40 seconds. Guyana is a rural country in the north-eastern corner of South America, with a population of around 740,000. It has recorded the highest suicide rates in the world for several reasons, the most significant of which are poverty, alcoholism and easy access to lethal pesticides. To better understand how risk factors interact, Franklin and his colleagues applied machine learning to the electronic health records of over 5,000 people with a history of self-harm. They developed an algorithm that predicted suicide attempts based on a range of risk factors, including demographic data, previous diagnoses, medication history and previous healthcare usage (Walsh et al., 2017). Franklin says: “Machine learning can take us from near-random guesswork to predictions that are about 80% accurate.” Therefore, through this intervention, we aim to determine the extent to which artificial intelligence can predict suicidal thoughts and, consequently, to attempt to identify mechanisms for preventing them and reducing the rate of suicide attempts.

items.title: The Role of Digital Transformation in Higher Education: Enhancing Human Capital to Achieve Sustainable Development in Syria
items.abstract: The world is witnessing a rapid digital transformation that imposes itself as a fundamental pillar for developing the efficiency of the educational system. In the Syrian context, this transformation acquires highly critical strategic dimensions; it is not merely an immaterial process or a modern luxury. Rather, from one perspective, it represents an essential tool to overcome the repercussions of crises and dismantle material relationships of digital dependency. From another perspective, it serves as a qualified vehicle for building human capital, paving the way for the sustainable reconstruction phase in line with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 2015. The research problem lies in the gap between the requirements of digital transformation and the actual reality of the higher education sector in Syria, which faces severe infrastructural, technical, and funding challenges. items.title: The Role of Social–Emotional Learning in Special and Inclusive Education: A Path Analysis Integrating Intrinsic Motivation, Efficacy, Stress, and Well-Being
items.abstract: Teaching in special and inclusive education presents unique emotional and ecological demands, yet the specific psychological mechanisms through which social–emotional learning (SEL) competencies relate to how teachers navigate these challenges remain underexplored. Therefore, the present study investigates the pathways linking educators’ SEL and intrinsic motivation to their psychological well-being. In this cross-sectional study, 459 educators completed self-report questionnaires assessing their SEL competencies, intrinsic motivation, teacher self-efficacy, perceived work stress, and psychological well-being. The findings show that both SEL competencies and intrinsic motivation are positively associated with teacher self-efficacy, which in turn is negatively related to perceived work stress and positively associated with psychological well-being. Furthermore, a multigroup path analysis comparing educators in special-education settings with those in inclusive environments revealed no statistically significant differences in these pathways between the two contexts. However, the substantial disparity in group sizes warrants cautious interpretation of this finding. By illuminating the interplay between internal socio-emotional resources and occupational stress, this research highlights the potential protective value of SEL competencies in relation to educator well-being across diverse and demanding educational contexts.

items.title: The Strengths and Weaknesses of Ten Global LLM and AI Knowledge Systems: A Comparative Monograph Through the Lens of cCC* and Natural Human Learning
items.abstract: Large language models have developed from fluent next-token generators into integrated systems capable of reasoning, coding, multimodal interpretation, retrieval, tool use and increasingly persistent agentic action. This monograph reviews ten influential global systems: OpenAI GPT-5-class ChatGPT, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, xAI Grok, DeepSeek, Moonshot Kimi, Alibaba Qwen, Mistral, Perplexity and Obsidian. They are not all equivalent objects. GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen and Mistral are model families; Perplexity is primarily a retrieval-and-research architecture that orchestrates models and sources; Obsidian is a human-owned knowledge environment in which language models may be embedded. The review therefore avoids a misleading single benchmark league table and instead compares eight dimensions: reasoning, factual reliability, coding and agency, multimodality, context and retrieval, openness and deployment, governance and safety, and support for durable human meaning-making. Published system cards and developer documentation show large gains in benchmark performance and reductions in factual error, but none establishes that probabilistic model competence is equivalent to human understanding, selfhood or conscious learning. The strongest common limitation is not simply hallucination. It is the absence of an explicit, inspectable architecture for the transition from observation to question, from question to perspective, from perspective to interpretation, from interpretation to choice, and from choice to reconstructed meaning. This is where cCC* is positioned as a research proposition rather than as another foundation model: Curiosity → Chances → Choices → Changes, interpreted through AEIOUF perspectives, SELF ↔ OTHER distinction, P M ΘΦ guardrails, and the recursive NEWCON → INCON → RECON → NEXT? cycle. The monograph concludes that current systems are increasingly powerful at producing and acting upon representations, while Natural Learning asks a different question: how does an embodied human observer construct, contest, share and recursively reconstruct meaning?

items.title: THE SYNTHETIC DATA PARADOX Evaluating AI-Generated Training Data for Model Performance, Diversity, Privacy, and
items.abstract: Synthetic data can support machine-learning research when real observations are scarce, sensitive, expensive, or difficult to share, but synthetic status and dataset size do not establish utility, representativeness, privacy, or fairness. This focused narrative review synthesizes selected research on generation methods, predictive utility, fidelity and diversity, subgroup representation, privacy, fairness-aware generation, recursive training, and large-language-model-generated data. The evidence indicates that suitability is conditional: generated data must preserve information relevant to the intended task, represent important and rare patterns, and be assessed for subgroup disparities and disclosure risks. Results from recursive-training studies further show that repeated reliance on generated data can reduce distributional coverage under some conditions, although the risk depends on the training setup and the availability of real data. Because the reviewed studies use different domains, datasets, methods, and metrics, they do not support a universal ranking of synthetic-data methods. The paper’s central contribution is a proposed integrated evaluation framework that brings together six dimensions—predictive utility, fidelity, diversity, subgroup fairness, privacy, and recursive-data risk—and explains why they should be considered together rather than treated as interchangeable measures. The review is narrative rather than systematic: sources were selected for relevance and influence, no exhaustive screening process was performed, and the synthesis is not a complete census of the field. The framework is conceptual and has not been empirically validated in this paper. The findings support use-case-specific evaluation, transparent reporting, subgroup analysis, documented data lineage, and direct assessment of privacy claims.

items.title: The Web of Stigmas: A Systematic Literature Review of the Impact of Different Types of Stigma on Occupational Risks in Sex Work
items.abstract: Objectives Stigma is an important structural determinant of occupational health and safety in sex work, whereby gaps remain in understanding the complexity of the phenomenon. This article examines anticipated, experienced, internalized, layered, perceived, and secondary stigmas, and explores how they affect occupational risks pertaining to sex workers’ access to services, private lives, health, violence, and careers. It also explores how stigmas are manifested in different legislative models regulating sex work.Methods A PRISMA-guided systematic review of peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2010 and 2020 was conducted using a centralized academic search system enabling simultaneous searches across major databases and publisher platforms, such as Web of Science, Scopus, JSTOR, SAGE, EMERALD, PubMed, MEDLINE, ScienceDirect, and EBSCO. A total of 90 qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods studies published globally met the eligibility criteria and were analyzed through systematic data extraction and coding.Results The results demonstrate that stigma functions as a complex system of discrimination in which different types of stigma operate simultaneously across occupational domains. The evidence most consistently highlights the negative effects of experienced, anticipated, and internalized stigmas, particularly regarding access to services and impacts on private life. Occupational risks where different stigmas most intensely intersect include increased vulnerability for STIs, mental distress, and barriers to the utilization of services. The reviewed studies further suggest that stigma-related occupational risks may manifest differently across legislative models, with more adverse effects reported in criminalizing and otherwise repressive legal contexts.Conclusions Different types of stigma intersect and build an interconnected web transcending occupational risks and legislative models concerning sex work. Our findings emphasize the need to address stigma as critical occupational risk that requires sustained research and targeted policy interventions, conceptualizing it as a complex, structural, and intersectional phenomenon.

items.title: Think, Compress, Answer: Reinforcement Learning for Multimodal Grounding via Reasoning Compression
items.abstract: Extended reasoning has substantially improved multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on tasks requiring compositional and relational inference. However, multimodal grounding imposes a distinct requirement: reasoning must ultimately converge on a target-specific compact representation that supports precise localization. As reasoning trajectories grow longer, they often expand into broad scene narratives and peripheral relational details, which can dilute grounded perceptual evidence and lead to ambiguous or incorrect predictions. Motivated by the information bottleneck principle, we propose Think-Compress-Answer (TCA), a reinforcement learning framework that decomposes multimodal grounding into three phases: free-form reasoning, target-aware context compression, and answer generation conditioned on the compressed context. TCA is optimized through a multi-stage Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with progressive rewards that establish the structured output protocol, minimize reasoning-specific information while preserving target-relevant content, and directly improve localization accuracy. This staged design enables MLLMs to retain the benefits of extended reasoning while distilling it into the minimal context required for grounding. Experiments across six multimodal grounding benchmarks show that TCA attains substantial zero-shot performance gains, demonstrating the effectiveness of reasoning compression.

items.title: TimesJev: Thinking Fast on Time Series with System 1 Sufficiency
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown strong potential for time series reasoning, while models that reason over time series are usually with long chains of thought. However, this process often consumes thousands of tokens, directly leading to substantial latency during inference. In contrast, System 1 models such as Jev make decisions instantly and can naturally be an alternative, but raw time series are not compatible with the embedding space of these models, thus hindering the reasoning performance, especially when input series contain thousands of numeric points. In this paper, we make a very early attempt to propose a time series System 1 model, namely TimesJev. Specifically, we first formalize System 1 sufficiency in time series reasoning, which motivates a compressed representation for time series with key frequency patterns preserved. To construct this representation, we derive a dimension reduction objective that combines (i) a sufficiency divergence that measures the core information lost during compression, and (ii) a realizability divergence that quantifies the incompatibility of the System 1 model to the optimal prediction given this representation. We optimize this objective by learning time series compression with a gating mechanism for sufficiency, and then aligning the selected representation with the embedding space for realizability. Finally, experiments on 13 datasets demonstrate that TimesJev outperforms reasoning models by over 62% with 62.9% less inference time than their fine-tuned versions on average.

items.title: TokenGate: Adapting LLMs for Fast and Memory-Efficient Prefill with Learned Token Pruning
items.abstract: Expert human readers process large inputs (e.g., code repositories and long documents) by skimming to closely read only what matters. On the other hand, language models process all input tokens through each model layer, resulting in significant processing costs for long-context inputs. We introduce TokenGate, a small, drop-in component that extends existing trained models to enable end-to-end learnable token pruning over long-context inputs for fast and memory-efficient prefill. To enable end-to-end learning despite the non-differentiable top-K operator for token pruning, we introduce token-gated attention, a mechanism inspired by Mixture-of-Experts that re-weights attention logits using token importance scores. Across diverse tasks, TokenGate achieves $1.4$-$11.3\times$ faster time-to-first token (TTFT) and $1.5$-$3.4\times$ lower peak memory at no accuracy degradation for prefill in transformers. Compared to the best-performing prior methods for token-pruning, TokenGate gives up to $6.4\times$ faster prefill and $2\times$ lower peak memory. TokenGate natively extends both standard transformers (e.g., Qwen3) and hybrid-attention models (e.g., Qwen3.5) with simple lightweight adaptation comparable to standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning. We make our code available at: https://github.com/tokengate-models/TokenGate.

items.title: Toward an AI- and learning-analytics-enabled inclusive support framework for students with learning difficulties in Kuwait's higher education institutions
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and learning analytics are transforming higher education by enabling personalised learning, adaptive support, and data-informed decision-making. These developments present significant opportunities for improving educational inclusion for students with learning difficulties, yet they also introduce challenges relating to privacy, algorithmic bias, explainability, accessibility, and governance. Although Kuwait has strengthened disability legislation while simultaneously investing in AI-enabled education under Kuwait Vision 2035, these policy agendas have largely evolved independently. Similar governance gaps are evident across the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), where disability inclusion, AI adoption, and higher education reform remain weakly integrated. This conceptual paper develops the AI- and Learning-Analytics-Enabled Inclusive Support Framework for Learning Difficulties (ISF-LD) to guide the responsible implementation of AI within inclusive higher education. Using a conceptual framework development methodology, the study synthesises evidence from four complementary domains: research on learning difficulties and disability inclusion; scholarship on AI, learning analytics, and responsible AI; national and international policy documents; and established educational and disability theories. The framework is informed by six theoretical perspectives: the Social Model of Disability, Universal Design for Learning, Sociocultural Theory, Self-Determination Theory, learning analytics ethics, and responsible AI principles. The proposed framework comprises five interconnected implementation layers: national policy and governance, institutional leadership and disability services, faculty capability, AI-enabled inclusive pedagogy and assessment, and student self-determination. These layers operate through an iterative, non-linear governance model in which each layer informs and is informed by the others, supported by four cross-cutting principles: rights-based governance, stigma-aware disclosure, universal accessibility, and responsible AI. Together, they position AI as a governed educational capability that supports inclusion while safeguarding learner autonomy, transparency, and institutional accountability. The paper contributes to the literature in three ways. First, it integrates disability studies, AI governance, learning analytics, and inclusive higher education within a single conceptual model. Second, it addresses an important policy gap by linking disability inclusion with AI governance in the context of Kuwait and the GCC. Third, it proposes a theoretically grounded and empirically testable framework that can inform institutional strategy, educational policy, and future research on responsible AI in higher education. Although developed within Kuwait, the ISF-LD offers a transferable governance model for universities seeking to implement AI ethically while advancing equitable and inclusive learning.

items.title: Toward Controllable Learner Simulation for Teacher Education: Benchmarking Skill-Profile Control in LLM Answer Behavior
items.abstract: Teacher preparation depends on deliberate practice with learners who have identifiable strengths and weaknesses, yet classroom experience accumulates slowly and is hard to standardize. Language-model-simulated students could offer scalable, repeatable practice, but only if a simulated learner can exhibit a specified answer-performance profile rather than behaving as a uniformly capable assistant. We introduce a benchmark for controllable learner simulation in school mathematics: the target condition is a binary vector of retained and suppressed curricular skill families, and we measure how faithfully a language model’s answer behavior realizes that profile via profile-alignment, retained-versus-forgotten, and cross-skill analyses. Across three models and two grades, selective suppression can be induced and measured, yet higher mathematical capability did not imply stronger controllability among the evaluated models: a model can solve the mathematics well yet be the weakest at selective suppression (bootstrap selectivity index 0.35 to 0.70). Induced errors are systematic: independent models converge on the same wrong answers, and an exploratory single-coder analysis found many compaible with documented error categories. Evidence is answer-level (single turn, multiple choice) at Grades 4 and 5. These results show that answer-level skill-profile controllability can be measured as one prerequisite for studying LLM-based learner simulation in teacher-preparation and assessment research.

items.title: Towards Architectural-Level Safety Control: Relocating Hazardous Knowledge into Removable Experts in Mixture-of-Experts Models
items.abstract: Large language models acquire broad knowledge from web-scale corpora during pretraining, including knowledge that could be hazardous if misused. Removing such knowledge from the model itself without degrading general capability is desirable but difficult, as it is deeply entangled with general capability within the same parameters. Existing safety alignment and unlearning methods typically adjust these shared parameters, tending to suppress the expression of hazardous knowledge rather than remove it. As a result, the knowledge remains in the model and is readily recoverable by subsequent fine-tuning. To address this limitation, we propose REX (Relocating into Removable EXperts), a knowledge relocation method that separates hazardous knowledge from general capability at the architectural level. Exploiting the modular structure of Mixture-of-Experts models, REX expands the model with a set of new, physically removable experts designated to hold hazardous knowledge. Through expert expansion, selective gradient masking and routing differentiation, it relocates hazardous knowledge out of the original experts and concentrates it in the new ones. Excising these new experts yields a model suitable for public release. This removal holds consistently across Intern-S2, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B; on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, for instance, excision lowers WMDP-Bio accuracy by 48.4 points while MMLU changes by less than 3 points. The excised model matches the strongest of nine unlearning baselines in removing hazardous knowledge, and it is the only one that preserves this removal under subsequent fine-tuning. After 250M tokens of standard fine-tuning on Qwen3.5, the best baseline rebounds on WMDP-Bio from 44.1% to 78.3%, whereas REX rises only from 32.4% to 42.8%.

items.title: Towards the Digital Transformation of Official Statistics in Latin America and the Caribbean: Evidence on the Use of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence from the 2024–2025 NSO Consultations
items.abstract: This study examines the adoption, use, and institutionalisation of big data and artificial intelligence in official statistics in Latin America and the Caribbean, drawing on the 2024 and 2025 International Consultations conducted with National Statistical Offices. The study combines questionnaire data from 15 responding countries in 2024 and 21 countries and territories in 2025 with qualitative evidence from in-depth interviews. It also proposes the Statistical Innovation Index, a composite indicator designed to approximate differences in the adoption, integration, and institutionalisation of big data and AI across NSOs. Results indicate a gradual consolidation of big data use, although applications remain concentrated in web scraping and satellite imagery, particularly for price, population, environmental, and agricultural statistics. AI adoption remains at an earlier stage: 39% of responding NSOs reported its use, mainly in data processing and other operational tasks. The maturity classification reveals substantial heterogeneity across the region, with most NSOs concentrated in early or emerging stages of statistical innovation. Findings suggest that progress follows a selective process in which exploratory initiatives are gradually filtered into a smaller number of sustainable applications. Institutional capacity, governance, infrastructure, and regional cooperation emerge as key enablers of this process. More broadly, the findings suggest that the transition from exploratory to operational uses of big data and AI reflects an evolving institutional role of NSOs, in which technological innovation is accompanied by new responsibilities for data governance, institutional coordination, and maintaining public trust in official statistics.

items.title: Towards the learning estate: from digital–physical to experience orchestration
items.abstract: Universities increasingly orchestrate teaching and learning through compound configurations that span spaces, devices, timetables and roles. As digital content and workflows increasingly shape physical estates, and vice versa, alignment frames overlook the compound, cross-host configurations already in motion. In this article we ask whether estate-level orchestration, rather than digital–physical alignment alone, should be the operative unit of design for planning and delivering student experiences across and beyond campus. We draw on three exemplars at a research-intensive university: (1) a theatre-scale interactive three-dimensional system, which streams or web-delivers interactive three-dimension into traditional lecture theatres and learners’ devices; (2) a high-fidelity virtual reality digital twin of a chemistry lab for pre-lab rehearsal; and (3) space-planning web apps for co-design and decision support. From these, we sketch a purpose-orientated, configuration-first stance and situate it within work on cyber-/smart-campus estates, learning ecologies, TPACK and postdigital perspectives. Beyond education, digital-first space planning is already operational at scale, including in automotive manufacturing (BMW Group), cultural architecture (Dubai Museum of the Future) and national infrastructure (National Grid’s Triton platform). Higher education has both the conceptual case and, in several respects, the enabling conditions to follow. Hence, we argue that the convergence of immersive, computational and spatial technologies is expanding what institutions can compose and deliver, making device-label categories less useful for both learning and space design. This configuration-first stance is also directly applicable to the governance of artificial intelligence in higher education: as with earlier technology labels, institutions risk misallocating attention and resource if ‘artificial intelligence’ is treated as a discrete category rather than as a family of capabilities, from generative code or audiovisual models to computer vision and wearable ‘artificial intelligence’, some of which already permeate the configurations described here. We conclude with operational implications and a call for institutions to transcend their siloed functions and budgets, by elevating orchestration (not devices, spaces or platforms) as the primary unit of design.

items.title: Training Controllable World Models via Action Influence Maximization
items.abstract: Action-conditioned video generative models trained on successful, goal-directed demonstrations tend to ignore the commanded action, rendering a plausible expert-like future regardless of what is asked of them. We trace this failure to training data that lack sufficient action influence. We analyze this metric and prove that it upper bounds the action influence that any model trained on that data can express. Expert demonstrations, whose narrow action distributions let next states be predicted without attending to the action, set a low ceiling that no amount of model capacity alone can raise. Raising it requires collecting different data. We introduce Action Influence Maximization (AIM), an algorithm for actively collecting training data for improving dataset action influence. We compare the performance and data-efficiency of AIM against exploration heuristics and intrinsic-motivation methods on simulated navigation and manipulation tasks. In pixel-based manipulation, AIM is the only method that consistently improves controllability: 500 actively collected episodes added to 3k demonstrations match a world model trained on 300k expert episodes on end-effector controllability, an $85\times$ reduction in data.

items.title: Training with ML-labeled Data via Stochastic First- and Zeroth-Order Optimization
items.abstract: Training a machine learning (ML) model is an optimization process that typically requires a set of examples with ground-truth labels beforehand. Obtaining these ground truths usually requires laborious human effort and can be costly. The scalability of human labeling becomes a concern when there are a large number of data points that need to be labeled. To address this practical issue, we consider an optimization setting where a subset of samples has ground-truth labels, while the remaining data points were labeled by an ML predictor, which could potentially assign incorrect labels to those points. We propose both first-order and zeroth-order stochastic optimization methods for training on datasets consisting of a mix of true-labeled and ML-labeled samples. We further conduct comprehensive empirical studies from training a linear regression model to fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) to showcase the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms for training with ML-labeled data.

items.title: Transformación en la comunicación académica y profesional de Ecuador y Perú, mediante la adopción de la IA
items.abstract: La expansión de la inteligencia artificial en la comunidad educativa y profesional está transformando la creación de contenidos, generando oportunidades y desafíos que requieren análisis contextualizados. Este estudio examina los niveles de conocimiento, frecuencia de uso y ventajas percibidas de la IA en usuarios de Ecuador y Perú, países con sistemas educativos comparables. Se aplicó una metodología cuantitativa mediante encuesta a 493 participantes, entre estudiantes universitarios y profesionales. Los resultados evidencian una relación positiva entre conocimiento y uso frecuente de IA, con diferencias por región, edad y género. Destaca el uso de herramientas generativas como ChatGPT y el crecimiento de Canva IA en creación visual, confirmando el impacto transformador de la IA en la comunicación académica y profesional.

items.title: Transition metal-mediated composite systems for peracetic acid-based AOPs in water treatment: Mechanisms, influencing factors, and application outlook
items.abstract: Peracetic acid-based advanced oxidation processes (PAA-AOPs) have garnered significant interest in water treatment due to the high efficiency, low toxicity, and minimal pH dependence. However, single transition metal catalytic systems often suffer from limited pH adaptability, surface passivation, metal leaching, and a narrow spectrum of reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. To overcome these bottlenecks, transition metal-mediated composite PAA-AOPs have been developed, which integrated synergistic components such as secondary metals, sulfur modifiers, reductants, chelators, or external energy inputs. This review systematically summarized the current development of these composite systems, with a focus on the construction strategies and underlying mechanisms for enhanced PAA activation. The synergistic effects driving bimetallic redox cycles, electron donation, metal-ligand complexation, and energy-assisted electron transfer were critically examined, alongside the generation pathways of both radical and non-radical ROS. Furthermore, the key factors governing process performance, like solution pH, catalyst and PAA dosages, reductant/chelator concentrations, and water matrix constituents were evaluated. The practical application potential of these systems was assessed in terms of catalyst stability, performance in real water matrices, and ecological toxicity reduction. Finally, this review offered prospects for future research, emphasizing the integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning to accelerate catalyst design and process optimization, advancing the development of intelligent, efficient, and low-carbon water treatment technologies.

items.title: TreeView: A Structured User Interface for Understanding, Verifying, and Extending Unfamiliar Computational Notebooks
items.abstract: Computational notebooks are widely used in data science for their interactive, flexible environment. However, their linear format can hinder comprehension, verification, and extension, especially when users engage with unfamiliar or poorly documented notebooks. We present TreeView, a JupyterLab extension that transforms the notebook into a semantically structured, execution-aware tree-like structure. By combining automatic exploratory data analysis (EDA) stage categorization, cell grouping and summarization, inline execution/output inspection, and natural language querying, TreeView provides a unified interface for high-level reasoning and in situ exploration. Through a controlled within-subjects study (N = 14), participants using TreeView completed tasks faster than with the traditional linear notebook baseline and achieved higher accuracy when identifying appropriate extension points. Participants also reported lower cognitive load and greater satisfaction, citing improved orientation, verification, and workflow continuity. Based on these findings, we discuss design insights for intelligent interfaces that support short-term sense-making and navigation in unfamiliar computational notebooks.

items.title: Trust and Adoption Intention Toward AI-Enabled IBM Cloud Services Among IT Professionals in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Artificial-intelligence-enabled cloud services are becoming increasingly important for digital transformation, but users may not adopt these services simply because they believe the technology is useful. This study examines the factors associated with adoption intention toward AI-enabled IBM Cloud services in Bangladesh, with particular attention to performance expectations, trust, technology readiness and digital skills readiness. The analysis uses the Group 5 survey database, which contains 400 records. After applying the prespecified attention-check criterion, 385 cases were retained for the main analysis. The database contains 30 five-point Likert-scale items representing 10 constructs: perceived usefulness, relative advantage, compatibility, innovation adoption readiness, performance expectancy, effort expectancy, trust, technology readiness, digital skills readiness and adoption intention. Descriptive statistics, reliability and measurement diagnostics, hierarchical regression, bootstrap analysis and importance-performance analysis were used to examine the data. Overall adoption intention was positive (M=3.79, SD=0.48). The full regression model explained 30.5% of the variance in adoption intention. Technology readiness was the strongest unique predictor (β=.224, p<.001), followed by performance expectancy (β=.157, p=.001), digital skills readiness (β=.147, p=.002) and trust (β=.140, p=.003). Adding the trust and readiness variables increased the explained variance by 11.6 percentage points (ΔR²=.116), showing that these factors provide important information beyond innovation attributes and UTAUT-oriented expectations. An exploratory indirect pathway was also observed: technology readiness was positively related to digital skills readiness, which was in turn related to adoption intention. The bootstrapped indirect effect was positive (ab=.067, 95% CI [.031, .108]). These findings suggest that AI-enabled cloud adoption is not only a question of perceived technological value; it also depends on whether users feel prepared, digitally capable and sufficiently confident in the cloud provider. However, all ten three-item scales showed Cronbach's alpha values below .70, and several discriminant-validity indicators were elevated. Therefore, the findings should be interpreted as data-grounded associations rather than as definitive confirmation of a latent-variable model. The main contribution of the study is a readiness-centered interpretation of AI-enabled cloud adoption in the Bangladesh context, together with a clear recommendation for future scale validation and confirmatory testing.

items.title: Trust of Pre-Service Teachers in Government Response to Gen AI Generated Deepfakes
items.abstract: This study examined the perceptions of pre-service teachers regarding the Spanish government’s response to the misuse of generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) for creating disinformation, as well as the mitigation of risks associated with deepfakes produced using these digital tools. A quantitative methodology was employed, involving 133 pre-service teachers pursuing a Primary Education degree in the Region of Murcia (Spain) who participated voluntarily. The results revealed low levels of confidence in the government’s response to these online threats. However, a minority of participants expressed greater confidence in the government and focused more on the risk of generative AI being misused to amplify manipulative disinformation campaigns. Raising awareness about the link between pre-service teachers’ knowledge of this issue and the government’s response could prompt educational authorities to take action and establish boundaries regarding the weaponisation potential of deepfakes. Specifically, further research within higher education programs is needed to help students master digital citizenship competencies that enable them to identify tactics of digital political manipulation, evaluate the motivations underlying the sources, and adopt preventive tracking mechanisms to rebuild the trust in authentic political information digitally accessible.

items.title: Unpacking the organizational commitment of fractional employees: the case of the C-suite executive
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the impact of protean and boundaryless career orientations on organizational commitment among fractional executives. This group represents a growing workforce segment that provides part-time and project-based executive services across multiple organizations simultaneously. Fractional executives are more likely to embody unique attitudes toward career progression and organizational loyalty. Design/methodology/approach The authors collected survey data from 169 fractional executives across diverse industries to examine how these career orientations influence affective, normative and continuance commitment. Necessary condition analysis (NCA) was used for data analysis. Findings The NCA analysis showed that protean attitudes, characterized by self-direction and values-driven motivation, were significant predictors of overall organizational commitment and, more specifically, of affective commitment. However, these attitudes were not necessary for continuance or normative commitment. Boundaryless career attitudes produced mixed results. Mobility preference predicted affective commitment, whereas psychological flexibility showed no significant relationship with continuance or normative commitment. Originality/value These findings advance understanding of leadership commitment in flexible work structures and offer practical insight for organizations engaging high-level fractional executives. The results stress the importance of aligning work design and leadership expectations with the career values of protean and boundaryless oriented professionals. They also provide practical guidance for organizations seeking to design fractional leadership arrangements that enhance commitment and performance. The study concludes with practical implications, limitations and avenues for future research.

items.title: Unsupervised Tool Evolution for Coding Agents in Data-Lake Analytics
items.abstract: Coding agents can answer analytical questions over a data lake by discovering, cleaning, and joining the relevant data. However, they discard this work after each question and redo it from scratch for the next one. Tool evolution, which automatically builds and refines reusable tools across tasks, is a natural fit for this repetition. Since a ground-truth label for a data-lake question requires an expert to solve it first, we consider the unsupervised setting. We propose TEAL (Tool Evolution for Analytics over data Lakes), which evolves a library of tools and usage skills for a given Worker agent without labels. Two agents propose tools from complementary evidence, an Explorer from the data lake itself and a Critic from Worker trajectories. A proposed change is kept only if the Worker adopts the tool on a rerun without extra steps and any changed answer is supported by trajectory evidence. We also introduce TEAL-Q, which generates synthetic questions for tool evolution when real ones are unavailable. We evaluate on KramaBench and LakeQA with four Worker LLMs under step budgets, which cap the number of steps the Worker may take per question. With a tight budget of 10 or 15 steps, TEAL improves every Worker on both benchmarks, lifting Sonnet-5 at 15 steps by 9.3 points on KramaBench and 21.7 points on LakeQA. A tighter budget also yields better feedback for evolution. For example, Sonnet-5's LakeQA library evolved at 20 steps and deployed unchanged at 30 steps scores 68.3, above both the baseline (59.6) and a library evolved directly at 30 steps (64.2). Additionally, a library evolved on synthetic questions performs comparably to one evolved on real questions. These results show that useful tools can be evolved without labels, and hopefully inspire future work on what to evolve and how to obtain feedback in unsupervised agent evolution.

items.title: Usability Challenges across AI-Assisted Infrastructure, Security, and Scientific Workflows
items.abstract: AI-assisted tooling is increasingly being integrated into infrastructure management, security operations, software engineering, and scientific computing environments. While discussion around AI adoption often emphasizes automation and productivity, expert users still need to understand what these systems are doing, decide when to trust their recommendations, and know what to do when the system is wrong or uncertain. This talk synthesizes findings and observations from UX research across enterprise data classification, identity and access management (IAM), backup and recovery, ransomware resilience, and AI-assisted infrastructure workflows. The evidence includes studies with cloud developers, security and compliance practitioners, and IT and site reliability professionals, alongside ongoing design and research work examining how expert users interact with AI-supported technical systems. Across these domains, three recurring usability challenges emerge: unclear system state, difficulty evaluating AI-generated recommendations, and limited support for correcting or recovering from AI-supported actions when something goes wrong. Although the technical environments differ, users repeatedly need to understand what the system observed or changed, evaluate whether a recommendation is appropriate for their specific context, and determine what to verify, reverse, or escalate before taking consequential action. These challenges have direct implications for research software engineering. AI-assisted code generation, workflow scripting, cloud and HPC configuration, notebook assistants, debugging, testing, and scientific automation introduce similar questions about visibility, trust, accountability, and recoverability. Lessons from enterprise infrastructure and security therefore provide useful design considerations for RSEs evaluating or building AI-assisted research software. The session offers a cross-domain synthesis of these recurring human-AI interaction challenges and practical questions for evaluating AI-assisted systems. Attendees will leave with a set of questions they can use to evaluate AI-assisted systems: whether users can understand system state, decide when to rely on a recommendation and when to question it, intervene when necessary, and verify or recover from the resulting actions. Connection to Mission, Goals, & Interests of US-RSE Community This talk aligns closely with the USRSE’26 theme, “Advancing Science in the Age of AI,” by focusing on the human and operational challenges that emerge as AI-assisted tooling is integrated into technical and scientific workflows. My background is in UX research and human factors across enterprise infrastructure, cloud systems, security tooling, and scientific software environments. Across these domains, I have observed the same challenges emerge when expert users interact with AI systems, including issues with transparency, trust calibration, oversight, error recovery, and workflow integration. While conversations around AI often emphasize capability and productivity, this session examines how usability and human-centered design influence the successful adoption of AI within complex environments. These topics are directly relevant to research software engineers who develop, evaluate, maintain, or adopt AI-assisted tools as part of scientific workflows. The goal of this session is to encourage discussion around designing AI systems that better support expert users while maintaining reliability, transparency, and human understanding. These topics connect strongly with the US-RSE community’s broader interests in sustainable, usable, and effective research software.

items.title: Use of a GenAI-patient for medical communication training for undergraduate medical students—a quasi-experimental study
items.abstract: Background Effective communication is fundamental to high-quality healthcare. Communication skills training is a core component of medical curricula, yet opportunities to practice with standardized patients (SPs) are limited, costly, and can elicit anxiety in novice learners. Generative AI (GenAI) virtual patients may offer a scalable and accessible supplement. This quasi-experimental study examined the effect of practicing with a GenAI-patient on medical students’ self-reported nervousness, preparedness, self-efficacy, and self-perceived competence during their first SP encounter. Materials and methods First-year medical students ( n = 383) at the University of Amsterdam were allocated on the basis of the class schedule to a control group receiving standard e-learning preparation ( n = 182) or an intervention group offered voluntary additional access to a GenAI-patient built on a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) framework using GPT-4o ( n = 201). Students completed a 31-item questionnaire after their first SP class. Primary outcomes were nervousness, preparedness, self-efficacy, and self-perceived competence. Group differences were assessed using Mann–Whitney U tests with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. The primary analysis was by intention-to-treat, comparing all students allocated to the intervention with all control students; the comparison restricted to actual users of the tool was secondary. Results Of 180 students that completed the questionnaire, 84 were controls and 96 students were allocated to the intervention, of whom 49 had used the GenAI-patient. No statistically significant differences were found between groups on the outcomes after FDR correction. In the intention-to-treat analysis; all composite effect sizes were near zero (Cliff's delta −0.05 to 0.04, all 95% confidence intervals including zero), as were those in the per-protocol comparison (−0.12 to 0.07). Among tool users, experience was generally positive: 63%–71% gave positive ratings. The majority considered the GenAI-patient a valuable contribution to the standard class preparation (71%). Conclusions Voluntary, single-session text-based practice with a GenAI-patient did not significantly reduce nervousness or improve self-assessed communication competence before a first SP encounter. Positive user experience suggests potential for the format, provided future iterations incorporate mandatory minimum engagement, multiple patient cases, automated feedback, and higher-fidelity multimodal interaction.

items.title: Use of AI in research
items.abstract: This lecture for MSc students in aerospace engineering presents a workflow for research with AI agents, from the author's evaluation of large language models between ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 3, Gemini 3.1, and Claude Opus 5.5. A use case shows an agent building a verified and validated Abaqus model of the double cantilever beam benchmarks of Krueger (2008) in one morning, with the researcher answering the decisive questions at checkpoints. The lecture discusses the responsible use of AI, how AI changes highly technical work, the growing role of experiments, and what this means for junior engineers. Lecture Given on 19 October 2026 as part of the Aerospace Structures and Materials core, Faculty of Aerospace Engineering, Delft University of Technology, Delft, The Netherlands. Contents Motivation for this lecture: why, after evaluating the new large language models every summer, Claude Opus 5 (August 2026) changed the author's way of working, and why the lecture was given now. Learning objectives: understand, evaluate and apply the author's way of working with novel AI models; create your own way of working with them; re-evaluate the role of a junior engineer in a world with AI. A brief history of large language models: from GPT-1 (2018) to GPT-4 (2023). How AI entered my research/education workflows: ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 3, Gemini 3.1, Claude Opus 5 and Claude Opus 5.5, and an analogy of three kinds of helpers. What fits inside current LLMs: tokens, context windows measured in papers, parameters against context, and the context of one agent session. Responsible use of AI: three rules, with a discussion: "Everything that can be automated should be automated"; "Focus on the crucial things, avoid the trivial things"; "Never delegate the decisions that make your work yours". My workflow with AI: a working folder in an integrated development environment, Claude as the agent, an HPC cluster as the simulation environment, and the state of the work kept in files (README, DECISIONS, REPORT), not in the chat. Consequences of a workflow with AI: how research moves forward through verification, validation and new hypotheses; where AI can take over parts of this process; what changed in the author's work. Use case: a verified DCB model: the prompt (goal, ten ground rules, phases with checkpoints), one morning by the clock, and where the model stood at the end of it. Figures as code: TikZ: vector figures written by the agent from the models' own data. How has AI changed highly technical jobs: numerical work and theoretical research; the shift from executing calculations to synthesis and verification; why experiments matter more, including AI combined with mechanical testing. The AI workflow of a junior engineer: how engineers grew until about 2024, judging what the AI produces, and two discussions. Take-home messages. The use case The agent built an Abaqus model of the double cantilever beam (DCB) benchmarks of the NASA report by Krueger (2008), NASA/TM-2008-215123, following a prompt written as a contract: every value with its source, every analysis through scripts, failed runs kept, and stops at two checkpoints where the researcher decides. In one morning, the agent completed the environment check and the reference card (09:46 to 10:07), wrote the plan after the researcher's decisions at the first checkpoint (11:23 to 11:29), and built and verified the model after the second checkpoint: the first models ran at 12:07, and the model worked at 13:23. At that point, the unidirectional model agreed with the published Marc 3D results of Orifici and Krueger (2010) within 0.1 to 0.6 %, and with the 2008 report within 0.1 to 0.8 % once its crack fronts were taken 0.5 mm beyond the labelled lengths; the acceptance criterion of the approved plan was 2 %. Running the use case The file use-case.zip contains the prompt of the use case, PROMPT_use_case.md. The report it works from is not included; to run the use case: Download the report by Krueger (2008), NASA/TM-2008-215123, from the NASA Technical Reports Server, where it is available free of charge: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20080015439. In your project folder, create a subfolder named references and save the report there as references/krueger2008NASA.pdf. The file name is the key of the case: if the agent does not find this file, it stops and asks. Place the prompt in the project folder, and check that its cluster settings suit your environment: ground rule 4 submits every analysis with qsub, and Phase 0 loads Abaqus in the cluster. Open the project folder with an AI coding agent (in the lecture: Claude, in an integrated development environment), and ask it to read the prompt and start with Phase 0. The agent creates the case folder krueger2008NASA_dcb next to references, and stops at two checkpoints for your decisions. Requirements: Abaqus with a valid licence, including its Python for scripting and post-processing; a computer or cluster to run the analyses; and Python for the work outside Abaqus, such as digitising figures. Take-home messages Write the prompt as a contract: definitions, ground rules, phases, and checkpoints where the agent stops and asks. Keep the state in files (README, DECISIONS, REPORT), not in the chat: someone else can reproduce every number. Automate everything that can be automated, and keep the focus on the crucial things. Let the agent verify and look for evidence; you judge the evidence. Delegate the implementation and the evidence for verification; keep the validation, the new hypotheses and the decisions at the checkpoints. Numerical work is increasingly automated, and theory is reaching automated scale: the work shifts to synthesis and problem definition, and to verification and auditing, and experiments matter more. For junior engineers: invest in the fundamentals; make a real effort to check what the AI produces against independent references; if you are not sure about a decision, study and talk to more experienced peers. Questions for discussion What do you consider a responsible use of AI? Which tasks of your work are trivial, and which are crucial? Which decisions make your work yours? In the process of doing research, where do you think we can delegate to AI? How can a recently graduated student judge what the AI produces and answer the decisive questions? How can a junior engineer work in synthesis and problem definition, and in verification and auditing of what an AI model does and produces, without the experience of a senior engineer, and without the chance to gain it the conventional way? About the file Two files, in English: the lecture slides (PDF): every click of the presentation is a separate page, and the sources cited on the slides are listed in full at the end; use-case.zip: the prompt of the use case (see Running the use case above). items.title: Use of Large Language Models (LLM) for Occupational Classification: An example of Early Learning & Child Care (ELCC) Workers
items.abstract: IntroductionThe use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for occupational classification has drawn the attention of statistical agencies because manual coding is time-consuming and expensive. In Canada, the national "$10-a-day" Early Learning and Child Care (ELCC) program has increased the need for more detailed information on the ELCC workforce. ObjectivesGiven the successful use of Machine Learning (ML) for occupational coding in open-ended Census write-in responses, this study explored the feasibility of creating an in-context ML classification protocol with a particular focus on Canada's growing ELCC sector. MethodsUsing Canada's 2021 Census of Population, write-in responses (n = 57,135) were classified using a large language model (LLM) for few-shot learning classification, an ML paradigm where a model is instructed to perform a task with a limited number of examples. Data were processed with Meta AI's Llama 2 model. ResultsExisting National Occupational Classification (NOC) and North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) categories are not sufficiently specific for the identification of a group of ELCC workers that is meaningful for policymakers. Through subject-matter expertise and iterative LLM classification reviews, NOC occupational groups were refined into several subgroups to better classify jobs relevant to the sector. Assigning workers to these refined subgroups would otherwise have been an inefficient and onerous undertaking through typical manual classification methods. ConclusionsThis study demonstrates the utility of LLM classification as an efficient and time saving tool. However, the tool cannot offer improvements in isolation and needs to be complemented by subject-matter expert input. The use of LLM resulted in a more granular and meaningful occupational classification for ELCC workers.

items.title: Using a smart compression sleeve to measure ergonomic risk in automotive manufacturing
items.abstract: BackgroundWork-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) are a significant concern in industrial settings, where repetitive and awkward movements contribute to ergonomic risk. Quantifying this risk allows for a better understanding of operator movement patterns and potential adjustments that can aid in injury risk mitigation.ObjectiveTraditional observational methods, specifically the Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA), provide ergonomic risk assessments but are limited by observer subjectivity and an inability to calculate movement durations. With wearable technology, precise kinematic and temporal data can be collected. The objective of this paper is to determine the feasibility of using wearable technology in place of video-based assessment for conducting ergonomic assessments.MethodsTo compare the effectiveness of these two methods, data was collected on an operator simultaneously by a smart compression sleeve and a video-based assessment system. This data was analyzed to calculate a risk score based on the RULA, which is used to provide an in-depth understanding of operator movements.ResultsThe video-based assessment system produced an assessment score of 3 for both trials, whereas the smart compression sleeve produced an assessment score of 2.62 for trial 1 and 2.93 for trial 2.ConclusionsThe wearable compressive sleeve demonstrated feasibility in the single-subject pilot study, with the ability to provide near-constant measurement if desired. A more comprehensive understanding of operator kinematics can aid in lowering ergonomic risk and therefore helping to mitigate potential WMSDs. Further research is needed to continue to refine the data processing efficiency and feasibility of long-term use.

items.title: Using AI to Build Student Feedback Literacy and Leverage Assessment as a Learning Tool
items.abstract: This conceptual article explores practical ways in which college and university instructors can leverage artificial intelligence (AI) to support assessment as learning and develop students’ feedback literacy. Traditional assessment practices often focus on assessment for learning (informing instruction) or of learning (measuring outcomes), while assessment as learning—when students actively monitor and reflect on their own learning—receives less attention. AI can help instructors leverage assessment as a learning tool by generating work samples for student analysis and providing timely, actionable feedback that students can use to revise their work. When combined with instructor modeling, peer dialogue, and scaffolds such as guiding questions or graphic organizers, AI-supported feedback promotes metacognition, self-directed learning, and critical evaluation skills. The article provides practical guidance, including prompts and strategies for using AI to enhance student engagement with feedback, helping instructors create more efficient, effective, and student-centered practices that utilize assessments as learning tools.

items.title: ValiAssist: Scaling LLM-generated Programming Feedback Validation by Demonstration
items.abstract: Generative AI can create programming feedback at scale, but validating its alignment with instructors' pedagogical goals and strategies remains challenging. Instructors may struggle to fully specify validation criteria upfront, as these often emerge through inspecting concrete examples and revising misaligned feedback. We present ValiAssist, a validation-by-demonstration system that infers reusable validation logic from instructors' revisions of AI-generated feedback and allows instructors to inspect and refine that logic as it is applied across other student submissions. In a comparative study with 16 instructors, ValiAssist helped instructors create and refine validation criteria, producing feedback that better aligned with their pedagogical intent (91% vs. 57%) and more than doubling the accuracy of correcting problematic criteria (77% vs. 32%). Our findings suggest that validation by demonstration can help instructors turn judgments they know how to make on individual cases into explicit, reusable logic, while progressively clarifying where those judgments do and do not generalize.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

items.title: Variation in Medical Ethics Recommendations Across Large Language Models: Case-Based Audit Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into clinical decision support, ranging from documentation aids to triage and patient communication. However, their behavior in ethically ambiguous medical situations is poorly characterized. Variability in how different LLMs balance approval of against refusal of a proposed action could materially shape the recommendations clinicians receive, yet no widely shared benchmark systematically quantifies this variability across contemporary model families. OBJECTIVE This study aimed to develop a standardized case-based audit set of medical ethics dilemmas and quantify variation in recommendation direction, model-reported confidence, within-model stability, and between-model agreement across 5 selected contemporary LLMs. METHODS We constructed 60 original medical ethics dilemmas spanning 4 domains. Three researchers independently annotated case difficulty and ethical principles before reaching consensus. Five primary models—GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, full-size DeepSeek-R1, and Meta Llama-3-8B-Instruct—were each evaluated 3 times per case using a fixed prompt and temperature 0. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B was evaluated separately as an exploratory small-model comparator. The primary outcome was the binary yes or no answer; model-reported confidence and reason were also collected. Model differences were assessed using a case-clustered generalized estimating equation (GEE), and between-model agreement and within-model stability were summarized. RESULTS Of 900 planned primary panel outputs, 897 (99.7%) had valid binary answers. Trial-level yes rates were 44.4% (80/180) for DeepSeek-R1, 42.4% (75/177) for Claude Sonnet 4.5, 38.9% (70/180) for GPT-5, 38.9% (70/180) for Gemini 2.5 Pro, and 16.7% (30/180) for Llama-3-8B. The overall model effect was significant (Wald χ24=23.34; P<.001); after Holm adjustment, only comparisons involving Llama-3-8B were significant. Across 59 complete-panel cases, raw agreement was 79.0% (466/590 model-pair comparisons; 95% bootstrap CI 72.9%-84.7%), and Fleiss κ was 0.55 (95% bootstrap CI 0.43-0.66). Within-model response stability across 3 runs ranged from 85.0% (51/60) to 100.0% (59/59 and 60/60). CONCLUSIONS Selected contemporary LLMs showed model-dependent variation but moderate overall agreement in binary recommendations for medical ethics cases. These results characterize recommendation behavior under a fixed, time-specific protocol and do not establish ethical correctness or the effects on clinicians or patients. Reporting model version, recommendation tendency, confidence, and repeatability may improve transparency when such systems are evaluated for ethically sensitive applications.

items.title: VeriCUA: Learning Proactive Verification for Reliable GUI Agent Rewards
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning for computer-use agents increasingly relies on proactive reward agents that interact with the post-execution GUI environment to verify what recorded screenshots cannot reveal. The reliability of such verification hinges on two coupled decisions: what to check and when to stop. Existing methods leave these decisions to prompted foundation models. However, neither scaling up the model nor providing few-shot examples reliably improves verification: prompted Judges ranging from 4B to GPT-5.4 all plateau at 68%-70% macro-average agreement. This is because the value of a check depends on the environment rather than the task alone, and becomes apparent only through execution. Learning from execution is itself constrained, as the Actor's terminal state cannot be faithfully replicated during training, allowing only one verification attempt per state. We introduce VeriCUA, a proactive reward agent that learns its verification strategy from these single attempts. A trainable Judge decides what to check and when to stop, while a frozen Probe executes the checks in the live environment. Online reinforcement learning optimizes the Judge for both verdict correctness and efficient Probe use, with returns normalized across terminal states. Trained only on OSWorld and evaluated without further training on MobileWorld and WebArena-Verified, VeriCUA achieves the highest reward agreement across all three benchmarks and lies on the agreement-cost Pareto frontier among proactive verifiers. It surpasses few-shot GPT-5.4 by 5.36 points with 47.6%-59.8% fewer Probe tokens, and even a 1B VeriCUA exceeds every prompted Judge. As the reward for Actor RL, it raises task success by 3.21 points overall and 5.40 points on held-out multi-application tasks. These results identify the verification strategy, not verifier scale, as the key to reliable GUI rewards.

items.title: Visual Memory and Textual Alignment for Cross-Modal Few-Shot Segmentation
items.abstract: Few-shot segmentation (FSS) aims to segment target objects with limited annotated examples. Recent studies have begun to explore large foundation models to improve generalization for this task. In particular, SAM 3 provides strong visual representations and supports text-guided segmentation. However, its performance remains limited in specialized domains, where semantic prompts and visual representations are often poorly aligned. To address this challenge, we propose ViTA-SAM, a framework built upon SAM 3 that integrates visual memory and textual features through cross-modal alignment. Specifically, we construct a visual memory module that encodes support features together with their corresponding masks, providing support-aware visual guidance for query prediction. In parallel, we leverage the text encoder of SAM 3 to extract semantic features as complementary priors. To bridge the gap between semantic and visual representations, we introduce a cross-modal alignment module that conditions textual features on memory-enhanced visual representations, yielding more consistent and visually grounded predictions. In addition, we propose a pseudo-label refinement strategy that updates the memory with predicted query masks, enabling query-adaptive representation learning. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show that ViTA-SAM achieves the best overall performance among the compared methods, outperforming the strongest competing method by over 5% in average mIoU.
